items.correctMeaning: Both say iron and nickel sank because they were more dense than the other materials. Canonical "than the materials around them" becomes "than the other materials"; the meaning is unchanged. The adapted stem glosses "molten" and splits one sentence into four.

distractorMisconceptions.A: Confuses temperature with density: assumes the hottest materials must be the ones that sink.
distractorMisconceptions.C: Thinks iron and nickel went to the center because they are magnetic, confusing the magnetic field with density as the cause of sorting.

items.correctMeaning: Identical correct option: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core. The stem splits the direction (surface to center) into its own short sentence.

distractorMisconceptions.A: Places the liquid outer core above the mantle (knows the crust is on top but not where the mantle sits).
distractorMisconceptions.C: Swaps the two core layers, the common error of thinking the liquid layer is at the very center.

items.correctMeaning: Both describe the crust as thin, brittle rock and the least dense layer. "A thin layer of brittle rock and the least dense layer" becomes "thin, brittle rock and the least dense layer".

distractorMisconceptions.B: Gives the crust the mantle's properties (thick, hot, slowly flowing).
distractorMisconceptions.C: Gives the crust the outer core's liquid iron and nickel, confusing layer composition and state.

items.correctMeaning: Identical correct option: oceanic crust sinks because it is more dense. The stem splits one long sentence into three short ones.

distractorMisconceptions.A: Thinks thicker crust is heavier and sinks, confusing thickness with density.
distractorMisconceptions.B: Knows oceanic crust sinks but reverses the density relationship, so the answer cannot be chosen from the crust name alone.

items.correctMeaning: Identical correct option: solid rock that can slowly flow. The stem changes only "statement" to "sentence".

distractorMisconceptions.A: The core misconception that the mantle is a layer of liquid magma.
distractorMisconceptions.C: Thinks solid rock cannot move at all, so misses that the solid mantle slowly flows.

items.correctMeaning: Both say the lithosphere is rigid (stiff) and broken into plates and the asthenosphere below it slowly flows. "Rigid" becomes "stiff", the lesson's own gloss for rigid, and each option is split into two short sentences.

distractorMisconceptions.B: Swaps the two zones: puts the flowing layer on top and the plates below.
distractorMisconceptions.C: Confuses the lithosphere and asthenosphere with the mantle and crust (mixes up the compositional and mechanical layer names).

items.correctMeaning: Identical correct option: hot rock is less dense than the cooler rock above it.

distractorMisconceptions.A: Reverses the density relationship that drives convection.
distractorMisconceptions.B: Thinks hot rock rises because it has melted into magma, the liquid-mantle misconception.

items.correctMeaning: Both say pressure from the layers above keeps the inner core's metal from melting. "From the layers above" is shortened to "from above"; the pressure cause is unchanged.

distractorMisconceptions.B: Uses a density explanation for the state of matter (and reverses the depth trend).
distractorMisconceptions.D: Credits the magnetic field, which the lesson ties to the core, with holding the metal solid.

items.correctMeaning: Identical correct option: released energy shakes the crust as an earthquake. The stem splits one sentence into three.

distractorMisconceptions.B: Confuses an earthquake with a volcanic eruption, both surface events caused by plate motion.
distractorMisconceptions.C: Thinks stuck plates fuse and stop instead of releasing energy when they slip.

items.correctMeaning: Both give the chain heat, mantle convection, plate motion, then earthquakes and volcanoes. Each option is split into short sentences; "internal structure" becomes "inner layers" in the stem.

distractorMisconceptions.A: Reverses cause and effect: plate motion heats the mantle instead of mantle convection moving the plates.
distractorMisconceptions.C: The liquid-mantle misconception: heat melts the whole mantle into magma that directly causes surface events.

showYourThinking.evidenceComparison: The adapted prompt and model answer are carried over unchanged from the owner-certified r1 presentation ap1fed..., because the canonical Show Your Thinking prompt and model answer did not change in the r2 authoring pass (canonical Show Your Thinking is lesson content, not part of the assessment revision; addendum 9.4). Both prompts ask for the same evidence: one or two sentences that explain, in order, the causal steps from the hot core to earthquakes and volcanoes at the surface, not a list of layers, using the word convection. The adapted prompt splits the canonical two sentences into five short ones and replaces "layered inner structure ends up causing" with "inner layers cause". It adds no step and removes none. The adapted model answer states the same chain as the canonical model (hot core, mantle convection, plate motion, surface change) and ends with the same success check. Its ending follows the lesson: stuck plates build pressure and suddenly slip, causing earthquakes, and in some places where plates meet or pull apart, rock below melts into magma that can erupt from volcanoes (not at every boundary). It also names density (hot rock is less dense and rises, cooler rock is more dense and sinks), which the canonical model implies with "rising and sinking material" and which the lesson's Convection Current KEY IDEA teaches. The success check does not add density as a requirement. Reviewer decision: whether naming density in the model answer is acceptable.
